content: Vital heat, also known as innate or natural heat (calidum innatum), refers to the internal heat generated within the body, primarily by the heart and the circulatory system. Ancient Greek physicians believed that this vital heat originated in the heart, was sustained by the pneuma (interpreted as spirit or soul), and was distributed throughout the body via blood vessels. These vessels were thought to function as intact conduits, using blood to transmit heat. Aristotle supported this concept by demonstrating that when the heart is cooled relative to other organs, death ensues. He theorized that the heat produced in the heart caused the blood to behave similarly to boiling liquid, expanding outward through the blood vessels with each heartbeat. However, he also warned that this intense heat could result in a self-destructive flame if it were not regulated and cooled by air from the lungs. Galen, in his work On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body (170 CE), described the heart as the hearthstone and source of the innate heat by which the animal is governed. This idea was later echoed by Avicenna in the 11th century. In his Canon of Medicine, Avicenna asserted that the heart was responsible for producing breath and the vital power or innate heat that sustains the body. By the 18th century, the concept of innate heat evolved. The Cyclopaedia (1728) attributed this heat to the friction generated by the movement of blood through the arteries, offering a more mechanical explanation for the phenomenon.
